paragraphs.heading: A hot climate with a dry spell
paragraphs.text: The tropical monsoon climate is a kind of tropical climate that the Köppen classification labels Am. It also goes by other names, such as sub-equatorial, tropical wet, or tropical monsoon and trade-wind littoral climate. Every month of the year averages above 18 °C (64 °F), yet there is still a dry season. It sits in the middle between the wet rainforest climate (Af) and the drier savanna climate (Aw).

paragraphs.heading: The driest-month test
paragraphs.text: The line between these climates is drawn by the rain in the driest month. For a monsoon climate, that month averages under 60 mm, yet stays above 100 − ((Total Annual Precipitation (mm))/25). A savanna climate's driest month is below both numbers. So a monsoon place usually gets more rain than a savanna, or has a gentler dry season, and its temperature also changes less over the year.

paragraphs.heading: When the dry month comes
paragraphs.text: The driest month nearly always arrives at the winter solstice or shortly after it. North of the equator that means the December solstice, and south of it the June solstice.

paragraphs.heading: The gentler version
paragraphs.text: In one form of this climate, the wet season brings huge amounts of rain, usually through frequent thunderstorms. Unlike most savannas, a fair amount of rain keeps falling in the dry season too, though not enough to count as a rainforest. Its dry seasons are therefore milder than a savanna's.

paragraphs.heading: The extreme version
paragraphs.text: Another form pairs a sharp dry season, much like a savanna's in length and feel, with a very rainy wet season. After the dry spell comes a long stretch, or several, of extraordinary rain. In some places a month can bring 1,000 mm of rain or more, two or more months running. Savannas generally do not get rain on that scale for so long.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is found
paragraphs.text: This climate is most common in Central America, in northern South America, in South and Southeast Asia, and in West and Central Africa. It also shows up in parts of the Caribbean, in South Florida and in northern Australia.

paragraphs.heading: The monsoon behind it
paragraphs.text: What controls this climate most is the monsoon, a seasonal change in the direction of the wind. In Asia, air flows onshore, from the ocean toward the land, during summer, the high-sun season. In the low-sun season, or winter, the air mostly flows offshore, from the land toward the water. The switch happens because water and land heat up in different ways.

paragraphs.heading: Africa and the Americas
paragraphs.text: Africa also sees shifting pressure patterns that make its rain seasonal, but they usually work differently from Asia's. When the sun is high, the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) brings rain, and when it is low, the subtropical high makes the weather dry. In Africa, and in the Americas too, monsoon climates usually sit along trade wind coasts.
